statement: The square on the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a fifth apotome.
heath_proof: Let AB be the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and CD a rational straight line, and to CD let CE be applied equal to the square on AB and producing CF as breadth; I say that CF is a fifth apotome. For let BG be the annex to AB; therefore AG, GB are straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial but twice the rectangle contained by them rational. [X. 77] To CD let there be applied CH equal to the square on AG, and KL equal to the square on GB; therefore the whole CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB. But the sum of the squares on AG, GB together is medial; therefore CL is medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line CD, producing CM as breadth; therefore CM is rational and incommensurable with CD. [X. 22] And, since the whole CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB, and, in these, CE is equal to the square on AB, therefore the remainder FL is equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB. [II. 7] Let then FM be bisected at N, and through N let NO be drawn parallel to either of the straight lines CD, ML; therefore each of the rectangles FO, NL is equal to the rectangle AG, GB: And, since twice the rectangle AG, GB is rational and equal to FL, therefore FL is rational. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, producing FM as breadth; therefore FM is rational and commensurable in length with CD. [X. 20] Now, since CL is medial, and FL rational, therefore CL is incommensurable with FL. But, as CL is to FL, so is CM to MF; [VI. 1] therefore CM is incommensurable in length with MF. [X. 11] And both are rational; therefore CM, MF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore CF is an apotome. [X. 73] I say next that it is also a fifth apotome. For we can prove similarly that the rectangle CK, KM is equal to the square on NM, that is, to the fourth part of the square on FM. And, since the square on AG is incommensurable with the square on GB, while the square on AG is equal to CH, and the square on GB to KL, therefore CH is incommensurable with KL. But, as CH is to KL, so is CK to KM; [VI. 1] therefore CK is incommensurable in length with KM. [X. 11] Since then CM, MF are two unequal straight lines, and a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on FM and deficient by a square figure has been applied to CM, and divides it into incommensurable parts, therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on MF by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CM. [X. 18] And the annex FM is commensurable with the rational straight line CD set out; therefore CF is a fifth apotome. [X. Deff. III. 5]

10.101
**Statement:** The square on the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a fifth apotome.

**Step 1.** Let c be the given straight line, and let r be the rational straight line to which its square is applied. By the designation in 10.77, write c = a − b, where a > b, the squares a² and b² are incommensurable, M = a² + b² is medial, and R = 2ab is rational. Here products denote rectangular areas. By 2.7, M = R + c²; hence M > R (CN5).

**Step 2.** Construct fourth proportionals p, q, h such that r:a = a:p, r:b = b:q, and r:a = b:h (6.12). Then rp = a², rq = b², and rh = ab (6.16). Put w = p + q and t = 2h. Thus rw = M and rt = R (2.1). Since M > R, the equal-base rectangles give w > t; subtracting them gives r(w − t) = c². Consequently w − t is the breadth in question (2.1, CN3, CN5).

**Step 3.** Since M is medial, its application to the rational straight line r gives w rational and incommensurable in length with r (10.22). Since R is rational, its application to r gives t rational and commensurable in length with r (10.20).

**Step 4.** The squares on w and t are each commensurable with the fixed rational square, and therefore with one another (D10.1.3, 10.12). Thus w and t are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). But t is commensurable in length with r, whereas w is not; hence w and t are incommensurable in length (10.13). Therefore w − t is an apotome, with whole w and annex t (10.73).

**Step 5.** The rectangles rp and rq have the same height, so p:q = rp:rq = a²:b² (6.1). Since a² and b² are incommensurable, p and q are incommensurable in length (10.11).

**Step 6.** Again using ratios of rectangles of equal height,

p:h = a²:ab = a:b = ab:b² = h:q

(6.1, 5.11). Reusing the rectangle criterion already employed in Step 2, we obtain pq = h² (6.16). Since t = 2h, we have t² = 4h² (2.4), and therefore pq is the fourth part of t².

**Step 7.** Since w = p + q, the rectangle contained by p and q is applied to w deficient by the square on q: indeed, wq = pq + q² (2.1). Its area is the fourth part of t², and it divides w into the incommensurable parts p and q. The direct path is therefore the incommensurable-cut criterion 10.18. Since w > t, that proposition shows that w² exceeds t² by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with w.

**Step 8.** We have an apotome w − t whose annex t is commensurable in length with the rational straight line r, while the square on its whole w exceeds the square on its annex by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with w. By D10.3.5, it is a fifth apotome. Since r(w − t) = c², the square on the given straight line, applied to r, produces as breadth a fifth apotome, as required.
